setup.caption: 3. Take turns. Put each card on a mat and say why.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 24 job cards and put them face down. 3. Put the lamp tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card is a job. For each job, we choose a material. Should it be transparent, so we see straight through? Translucent, so light comes in but no picture? Or opaque, so no light gets through?
flow.kid: Put out the three mats. Mix up the cards. For each job, pick a mat.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clear, Cloudy or Blocked?, a card game about choosing materials for jobs. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'A bathroom window'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. 'A bathroom window.' Which mat does it go on?
flow.kid: Practice card: a bathroom window. Clear, cloudy or blocked? Tap your answer.

good: We want light, but we want privacy too.

check.q: A bathroom window. What does it need?
check.why: A bathroom needs daylight, but nobody should see in. Translucent glass, like frosted glass, does both. Picking clear forgets about privacy. Picking blocked forgets that a window's job is to let light in.

flow.context: This is a practice round of the game Clear, Cloudy or Blocked?. You choose the right kind of material for a bathroom window.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out and puts it on a mat. 2. They say why. 3. They name one real material that would work. 4. Give a lamp token for each good reason.
flow.say: When you put your card down, tell me why, and tell me one real material that would do the job.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on a mat. Say why. Name a material. A good reason wins a 🪔 token.
flow.parent: Some cards are tricky on purpose. A greenhouse needs a transparent or translucent cover, because plants need light. A kite that glows needs translucent paper. A medicine bottle and a milk packet need opaque or dark material, because light spoils what is inside. A tracing sheet must be translucent, but thin enough to show the picture when it lies on top. A bird cage cover can be opaque, or thick translucent cloth. Accept any choice with a good reason.
flow.context: This is the main part of the game Clear, Cloudy or Blocked?. Players choose materials for everyday jobs and explain why.

flow.do: When a TRY IT card comes up, stop and do it together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we try it, everyone guess what will happen. Then we'll see who was right.
flow.kid: A TRY IT card! Guess first. Then try it. Were you right?

ask.q: Why did the oil spot on the paper go see-through?
good: The oil filled the little gaps in the paper.
Light did not scatter so much.

flow.think: Your hand lets a little red light through. So which mat does a hand belong on?
flow.context: This step of the game Clear, Cloudy or Blocked? is for the TRY IT cards, where everyone does a quick test with light.

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's tokens to find the winner. 2. Look at the three piles together.
flow.say: Look at the three piles. Were there any cards we argued about? Why could they go in two places?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Which card was hardest to place? Why?
flow.think: Is 'translucent' something a material is, or something it does to light?
flow.context: This is the last step of the game Clear, Cloudy or Blocked?. You find the winner and look back at the tricky cards.

games.title: Guess Behind the Sheet
games.players: 2 or more players, with a grown-up to work the torch
games.context: This is a guessing game. A torch shines on things from behind a white bedsheet. Players guess each thing from the shadow it makes. Opaque things make dark shadows, translucent things make pale ones, and transparent things make almost none. The bedsheet itself is translucent: light comes through it, but no clear picture.

printables.title: 12 object cards to cut out, for the hider
items: a cling film sheet on a frame
a hand making a bird shape

printables.title: Shadow score sheet
items: Dark, pale or almost no shadow?

rules: Hang a white bedsheet across a doorway, or hold it up between two chairs.
The hider stands behind the sheet with the torch and the objects. The guessers sit in front, in the dark.
The hider holds one object close to the sheet, with the torch about 2 metres behind it.
Guessers say what it is, and whether its shadow is dark, pale or almost none.
One point for the right object. One more for the right group: opaque, translucent or transparent.

setup.art: A white bedsheet pinned across a doorway in a dark room, with a torch shining onto it from behind.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a white sheet across a doorway. Make the room dark.

setup.art: Behind the sheet, a child holding a glass of water between a torch and the sheet.
setup.caption: 2. The hider holds one object between the torch and the sheet.

setup.art: From the front, the sheet shows a dark spoon shadow and a pale glass shadow with a bright line down the middle.
setup.caption: 3. The guessers look at the shadow and guess.

flow.do: 1. Hang a white bedsheet across a doorway, or between two chairs. 2. Switch off the lights. 3. Stand behind the sheet with the torch, about 2 metres back. 4. Put the objects on a stool beside you.
flow.say: I'll hold something behind the sheet, with the torch behind it. You'll only see its shadow. Guess what it is. Then tell me if its shadow is dark, pale or hardly there.
flow.kid: Sit in front of the sheet. A grown-up will hold things behind it. Guess each thing from its shadow.
flow.parent: Hold each object close to the sheet and keep the torch steady, about 2 metres back. Then the shadows are sharp. Never let a child stand on chairs to hang the sheet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Guess Behind the Sheet, a shadow-guessing game with a bedsheet and a torch. Here you set it up.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the objects one at a time, in any order. 2. Let the guessers shout their guesses. 3. Show each object after the guess. 4. Mark the score sheet.
flow.say: What is it? And is its shadow dark, pale or almost none?
flow.kid: What is it? Is the shadow dark, pale or hardly there? Say both.

ask.q: Why does the glass of water make a pale shadow with a bright line in it?
good: The glass is clear, so most light gets through, but its curved sides bend the light into a bright line.

check.q: The steel spoon made a very dark shadow. So the spoon is…
check.why: A dark shadow means almost no light got through. So the spoon is opaque. Picking translucent usually means mixing up 'shiny' with 'lets light through'. A shiny spoon sends light back, but none goes through it.

flow.context: This is the main part of Guess Behind the Sheet. You guess each object from its shadow.

flow.do: Swap. Let a child be the hider while the grown-up holds the torch.
flow.say: Now you choose something to hide. Can you find something that makes a pale shadow? Can you trick us?
flow.kid: Your turn to hide things. Can you find something with a pale shadow?
flow.think: A leaf made a pale shadow, and you could see its veins. Why do the veins look darker?
flow.context: This is the last step of Guess Behind the Sheet. Children take turns to choose the objects.

experiments.title: The Gap Test: how far until the words blur?
experiments.question: How see-through is each material? How far can we lift it off a page before we can no longer read the words?
experiments.predict: Before you test, line up the materials. Put the one you think you can lift highest first, and the one that blurs the word soonest last. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the material. Use the same card of letters, in the same light, and keep your eyes at the same height every time. Test each material 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Try 1: gap when the words blurred (cm)

materials.item: a card with the word LIGHT written on it in big letters, about 2 cm tall
pieces of 5 materials, each about as big as a postcard: cling film, a thin plastic carry bag, butter paper, a cotton handkerchief, a paper tissue
a ruler
a stack of books about 30 cm high, put right beside the card, to rest your chin on
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: This test is safe. Do it in daylight by a window, or under a bright room light. Never use the Sun directly.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Test each material 3 times. Write down the gaps. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each material. Make each bar as tall as its middle gap.
experiments.context: This is the gap test. You lay a material flat on a card of big letters, then slowly lift it. You measure how high you can lift it before the words blur. The higher you can lift it, the more see-through it is.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each material could be lifted before the words blurred
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different. Cling film never blurred, so we wrote the ruler's top, 30 cm.

setup.art: A card with the word LIGHT in big letters on a table, with a square of butter paper lying flat on top of it so the letters show through.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the material flat on the card of letters.

setup.art: A child resting their chin on a stack of books, lifting the butter paper slowly above the card with a ruler standing upright beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Keep your chin on the books. Lift the material slowly.

setup.art: A close-up of the ruler beside the raised butter paper, the letters below now blurry, a finger pointing at the 2 cm mark.
setup.caption: 3. When the word blurs, stop. Read the gap on the ruler.

flow.do: 1. Write LIGHT on a card in big letters, about 2 cm tall. 2. Cut postcard-sized pieces of the 5 materials. 3. Ask your child to put the materials in a line, from most see-through to least.
flow.say: Here are five materials. Which one do you think you can see through best? Put them in a line. Put the most see-through first.
flow.kid: Look at the five materials. Which can you see through best? Put them in a line. Best first.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: I can see my hand through it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the gap test. You will find out how see-through each material is, by lifting it off a page of words.

flow.do: 1. Put the card on the table near a window or under a bright light. 2. Stand the ruler upright beside it, with 0 at the table. 3. Make a stack of books next to the card. 4. Your child rests their chin on the books, so their eyes stay at the same height.
flow.say: We'll keep your eyes at the same height every time, so the test is fair. Rest your chin on the books.
flow.kid: Put your chin on the books. Keep it there the whole time. That keeps the test fair.
flow.parent: The chin rest matters. If the eyes move closer or further, the results change. Keep the room light the same for every try.
flow.context: This step sets up the gap test fairly: the same card, the same light and the eyes at the same height.

flow.do: 1. Lay the first material flat on the card. 2. Ask: can you read the word? 3. Hold the material by two edges, pulled gently tight, so it stays flat. 4. Lift it slowly, about 1 cm each second. 5. Your child says 'Stop!' the moment the word blurs so it cannot be read. 6. Hold still, read the gap on the ruler and write it down. 7. Do this 3 times for each material.
flow.say: Can you read the word now? Good. I'll lift it slowly. Shout 'stop' the moment you can't read it any more.
flow.kid: Can you read the word? Now watch it as the material lifts. Shout 'Stop!' when you can't read it.
flow.parent: Butter paper and tissue usually let you read the word when they touch the card, then blur within 1 or 2 cm. That surprises most children. If a material never blurs, like cling film, write the top of the ruler. To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.context: This is the main step of the gap test. You lift each material off the card until the word blurs, and measure the gap.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, with one bar for each material.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each material gets a bar. The taller the bar, the higher we could lift it before the word blurred.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each material. Make it as tall as its middle number. Taller means more see-through.

check.q: In the gap test, the plastic bag could be lifted 6 cm and the tissue only 1 cm. Which is more see-through?
check.why: The plastic bag could be lifted further before the word blurred, so it scatters light less. It is more see-through. Picking the tissue usually means thinking that a bigger number means more blur. Here the number is how high you could lift it and still read the word.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each material could be lifted before the words blurred
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like.

flow.context: This step of the gap test turns your measurements into a bar chart.

flow.do: Sort the five materials into transparent, translucent and opaque, using the results.
flow.say: Which material never blurred? That one is transparent. Which ones let light through but lost the word? Those are translucent. We tested nothing opaque. What could we add?
flow.kid: Which one never blurred? That is transparent. Which let light through but lost the word? Those are translucent.
flow.think: Butter paper let you read the word when it touched the card. So is it transparent when it touches, and translucent when it is lifted?
flow.context: This step of the gap test uses your results to sort the materials into transparent and translucent. None of the five was opaque.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now say three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: cling film is the most see-through. What I saw: the word never blurred with cling film, but with tissue it blurred at 1 cm. Why: the tissue has lots of tiny threads that scatter the light, and cling film is smooth all through.
flow.context: This is the last step of the gap test. You say what you found, the evidence, and why.

experiments.title: The Oil Spot Window
experiments.question: Can a drop of oil or water make paper more see-through? Does it last?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a drop of water make paper more see-through, less see-through, or the same? What about a drop of oil? Which will last longer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same sheet of paper for all three spots, so the paper is the same. Use one drop of each, the same size. Score all the spots in the same light.

materials.item: a sheet of plain white paper, like printer paper
cooking oil, like sunflower or groundnut oil (not coconut oil, which goes solid in cool weather)
a spoon of water
a dropper or a cotton bud
a newspaper or a printed page to read through the paper
a pencil

experiments.safety: Use a little oil only, and wipe up any spills so nobody slips. Wash your hands after.

schedule.what: Make a dry spot, a water spot and an oil spot. Score them. Wait one hour and score them again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with a score for each spot. 0 means you see nothing of the print. 1 means grey smudges where the print is. 2 means you see the shapes of words but cannot read them. 3 means you can read the words.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put a drop of water and a drop of oil on plain paper. Then you see whether each spot turns more see-through, and whether it stays that way.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper with three pencil circles labelled DRY, WATER and OIL.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three circles on the paper: dry, water and oil.

setup.art: A child putting one drop of oil in one circle with a cotton bud, and a drop of water in another.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of water in one circle and one drop of oil in another.

setup.art: The paper held over a newspaper: the words show clearly through the oil spot, less through the water spot, and hardly at all through the dry circle.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the paper over printed words. Score each spot.

flow.do: 1. Draw three circles on the paper, each as big as a coin. 2. Label them DRY, WATER and OIL. 3. Ask your child to guess what each drop will do.
flow.say: Paper is made of tiny threads with air between them. What do you think a drop of water will do to it? And a drop of oil?
flow.kid: Draw three circles. Write DRY, WATER and OIL. Guess what each drop will do.
flow.context: This is the first step of the oil spot experiment. You guess what a drop of oil and a drop of water will do to plain paper.

flow.do: 1. Put one drop of water in the WATER circle. 2. Put one drop of oil in the OIL circle. 3. Rub each gently with a clean fingertip so it spreads to fill the circle.
flow.say: One drop each. Rub it in gently, so it fills the circle.
flow.kid: Put one drop of water in its circle. One drop of oil in its circle. Rub gently.
flow.context: This step of the oil spot experiment puts the drops on the paper.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper over a newspaper page. 2. Score each circle from 0 to 3. 3. Then hold the paper up to a window and look at the light through each circle.
flow.say: Look through each circle at the print. Score it. Zero is nothing. One is grey smudges. Two is word shapes. Three is words you can read.
flow.kid: Put the paper on a newspaper. Score each circle from 0 to 3. Three means you can read the words.

check.q: Which spot let you see the newspaper words best?
check.why: The oil filled the air gaps between the paper threads. Light passes from thread to oil without bouncing much, so the words came through. Water works a little too, but less. Picking the dry spot usually means thinking that adding anything to paper must block more light.

flow.context: This step of the oil spot experiment scores how see-through each spot is, from 0 to 3.

flow.do: Leave the paper flat in a safe place for one hour.
flow.say: Now we wait one hour. What do you think will happen to each spot?
flow.kid: Leave the paper for one hour. Guess what will change.
flow.context: In this step of the oil spot experiment, you leave the paper for an hour to see if the spots change.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper over the newspaper again. 2. Score each circle again. 3. Compare with the first scores.
flow.say: Look again. Which spot changed? Why do you think the water spot went back to white?
flow.kid: Score each circle again. Which one changed? Why?

ask.q: Why did the water spot go back to white?
good: Air came back into the gaps.

flow.parent: The water spot usually goes back to white as it dries, because air fills the gaps again. The oil spot stays see-through, because oil does not dry away. Long ago, before glass was cheap, many people used oiled paper in their windows. Butter paper is made from pulp beaten very fine and pressed hard, so its threads pack tightly with few air gaps. That is why it is more translucent than ordinary paper.
flow.context: This step of the oil spot experiment checks the spots again after an hour.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: oil makes paper more see-through, and it lasts. What I saw: the oil spot scored 3 and stayed 3. The water spot scored 2, then went back to 1. Why: oil and water fill the air gaps, so light scatters less. Water dries away, oil does not.
flow.context: This is the last step of the oil spot experiment. You say what you found, the evidence and why.

experiments.title: Sunglasses Lab: when do they help?
experiments.question: Do sunglasses help us see better in bright light? Do they help indoors?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you read smaller letters with sunglasses on, or without, in bright light outside? What about inside a dim room? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same letter chart, stand the same 3 big steps away, and change only the sunglasses and the place.
results_table: Smallest row I can read without sunglasses
Smallest row I can read with sunglasses

materials.item: a pair of sunglasses from home, best with a UV400 label
a letter chart: six rows of letters on white paper, getting smaller, numbered 1 to 6
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun, with or without sunglasses. Sunglasses do not make it safe. A grown-up goes outside with you.

schedule.what: Make a letter chart. Read it outside in bright light, then inside in a dim room, with and without sunglasses.

experiments.record: Write the number of the smallest row you could read, each time.
experiments.context: In this experiment you read a chart of letters that get smaller and smaller. You read it with and without sunglasses, outside in bright light and inside in a dim room.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper with six rows of letters getting smaller, row 1 big and row 6 tiny, numbered down the side.
setup.caption: 1. Make a chart with six rows of letters, big to small.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the chart in a bright courtyard while a child stands three steps away in sunglasses, with their back to the Sun.
setup.caption: 2. Outside, stand 3 steps away. Read it with and without sunglasses.

setup.art: The same child in a dim room with curtains drawn, squinting at the chart with sunglasses on.
setup.caption: 3. Then do the same inside, in a dim room.

flow.do: 1. On white paper, write six rows of letters with a dark pen. 2. Make row 1 about 2 cm tall, then 1 cm, 7 mm, 5 mm, 3 mm and 2 mm. Use a fine pen for the small rows. 3. Number the rows 1 to 6.
flow.say: We'll make an eye chart. Each row has smaller letters. We'll see which is the smallest row you can read.
flow.kid: Write six rows of letters. Make each row smaller. Number them 1 to 6.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sunglasses lab. You make a chart of letters to test how well you can see.

flow.do: 1. Go to a bright balcony, terrace or courtyard in the late morning. 2. Hold the chart where the sunlight falls on it. 3. Your child stands 3 big steps away, with their back to the Sun. 4. They read the smallest row they can, without sunglasses, then with.
flow.say: Keep your back to the Sun. Never look at it. Read me the smallest row you can. Now put on the sunglasses and try again.
flow.kid: Turn your back to the Sun. Never look at it. Read the smallest row. Now try with sunglasses.
flow.parent: White paper in sunshine causes glare. Some children read one row smaller with sunglasses. Others see no difference outside. Both are honest results.
flow.context: This step of the sunglasses lab tests reading the chart outside in bright light.

flow.do: 1. Go into a dim room, with the curtains closed and one small light on. 2. Hold the chart 3 big steps away. 3. Your child reads it without sunglasses, then with.
flow.say: Now we're inside, where it's dim. Read the smallest row. Now with the sunglasses.
flow.kid: Now read the chart in a dim room. Then with sunglasses. Is it harder?

check.q: In the dim room, the sunglasses made the letters…
check.why: Sunglasses are tinted. They let only part of the light through. In bright sun that cuts glare. In a dim room there is little light to start with, so cutting it makes reading harder. Picking 'easier' usually means thinking that sunglasses always help you see. If you saw no difference, the room may not have been dim enough.

flow.context: This step of the sunglasses lab tests reading the chart in a dim room.

flow.do: Look at the label on the sunglasses together. Look for 'UV400' or '100% UV protection'.
flow.say: The darkness of the lenses is one thing. Blocking ultraviolet light, which we can't see, is another. The label tells us which.
flow.kid: Find the label on the sunglasses. Does it say UV400? That means they block ultraviolet light.
flow.parent: Dark lenses without ultraviolet protection can be worse than none. Behind dark lenses the pupils open wider, so more ultraviolet light gets in. Cheap toy sunglasses often have no ultraviolet filter.
flow.context: In this step of the sunglasses lab you check whether the sunglasses block ultraviolet light, the invisible light that can harm eyes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: When do sunglasses help? When do they get in the way? What did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: sunglasses help in bright sun, but not indoors. What I saw: outside I read row 5 with sunglasses and row 4 without. Inside I read row 4 without and only row 2 with them. Why: they let only part of the light through. That cuts glare in sun, but leaves too little light indoors.
flow.context: This is the last step of the sunglasses lab. You say what you found, the evidence and why.

activities.title: Glowing Hands and the See-Through Hunt

materials.item: a torch, or a phone torch
three bowls or trays labelled TRANSPARENT, TRANSLUCENT and OPAQUE

activities.safety: Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Only touch things you are allowed to carry.

schedule.what: Make your fingers glow with a torch. Then hunt the house for transparent, translucent and opaque things.

activities.record: Draw your glowing hand. Then list four things you found for each group.
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You make your fingers glow red with a torch, then hunt the house for things that let light through, scatter it or block it.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding a torch under their fingertips, which glow red.
setup.caption: 1. In a dark room, press a torch under your fingertips.

setup.art: Three trays labelled TRANSPARENT, TRANSLUCENT and OPAQUE on a floor, holding a glass, a sheet of butter paper and a steel plate.
setup.caption: 2. Set out three trays: transparent, translucent and opaque.

setup.art: A child holding a plastic bottle up to a window to see if light comes through.
setup.caption: 3. Hold each thing up to the light. Put it on a tray.

flow.do: 1. Make a room as dark as you can. 2. Your child presses the front of the torch against the tips of their fingers and switches it on. 3. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: Look at your fingers. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Press the torch under your fingertips. Switch it on. What do you see?

good: I can see darker lines inside.

flow.parent: The red glow is light passing through skin and blood. Red light gets through best. Don't explain much yet. Let the child wonder.
flow.context: This is the first step of the glowing hands activity. You find out that some light can pass through your own hand.

flow.do: 1. Put out the three labelled trays. 2. Your child collects things from around the house. 3. They hold each one up to a window or the torch. 4. They put it on the TRANSPARENT, TRANSLUCENT or OPAQUE tray.
flow.say: Find things around the house. Hold each one up to the light. Can you see clearly through it? Then it is transparent. Does light get through, but no clear picture? Then it is translucent. No light at all? Then it is opaque.
flow.kid: Find things in the house. Hold each to the light. See clearly through it? Transparent. Light but no picture? Translucent. No light? Opaque.

check.q: You hold a plastic carry bag up to the window. Light comes through, but the tree outside looks blurry. Which tray?
check.why: Light gets through, but the picture is blurry. That is translucent. Picking transparent usually means noticing the light but not checking the picture. Picking opaque forgets that some light did come through.

flow.context: This step of the hunt activity sorts things from around the house into transparent, translucent and opaque.

flow.do: Look at the three trays together.
flow.say: Was anything hard to put on a tray? Where would your hand go?
flow.kid: Look at your trays. Which thing was hardest to sort? Where does your hand go?
flow.think: Is your hand translucent or opaque? Does it depend on the light?
flow.context: This is the last step of the hunt. You look back at the trays and the tricky things.

activities.title: Where Did the Sugar Go?

materials.item: a clear glass of water from the tap
two teaspoons of sugar
a spoon for stirring
a small dark plate

activities.safety: This is safe. Plain tap water works. The sugar needs a minute or two of stirring to dissolve.

schedule.what: Look at a pile of sugar. Stir it into water. Watch the white vanish.

activities.record: Draw the sugar before, during and after stirring. Draw the tiny pieces you can't see, too.
activities.context: In this activity you stir white sugar into water and watch it vanish. It shows why piles of tiny grains look white, but the same sugar dissolved is clear.

setup.art: A small white pile of sugar on a dark plate next to a clear glass of water.
setup.caption: 1. Put a little pile of sugar on a dark plate.

setup.art: A spoon stirring sugar into a glass of water, the water cloudy with swirling grains.
setup.caption: 2. Tip the sugar into the water and stir.

setup.art: The same glass now completely clear, with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny sugar molecules spread among water molecules.
setup.caption: 3. Keep stirring until the water is clear again.

flow.do: 1. Put a little pile of sugar on the dark plate. 2. Look at one grain closely. 3. Then look at the whole pile.
flow.say: Look at one grain of sugar. It's almost clear, like a tiny bit of glass. So why is the pile white?
flow.kid: Look at one sugar grain. It is almost clear. But the pile is white. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the sugar activity. You look at sugar grains and wonder why a pile of clear grains looks white.

flow.do: 1. Tip the sugar into the water. 2. Stir slowly. 3. Watch until the water is clear.
flow.say: Watch the water while you stir. What happens to the white?
flow.kid: Tip the sugar in. Stir slowly. Watch the white disappear.

check.q: Why does a pile of sugar look white, when each grain is almost clear?
options: Sugar is painted white in the factory
Light bounces off the edges of every grain
The grains make their own light
check.why: Each grain has edges. Light bounces off each edge a little. With thousands of grains, the light is scattered every way, so the pile looks white. In water, the sugar breaks into molecules too small to scatter light, so the water is clear. Picking 'painted' is a fair guess, but big sugar crystals called mishri are much clearer, so sugar is not white inside.

flow.context: This step of the sugar activity stirs the sugar into water and asks why the white vanishes.

flow.do: Let your child taste a sip of the water.
flow.say: The sugar is invisible now. Is it gone? Taste and see.
flow.kid: Taste a sip. Is the sugar gone? Or is it still there, just too small to see?
flow.parent: This links to the Roots card, where a teacher in an old Indian book dissolves salt in water to make the same point. The sugar is everywhere in the water, but no light shows it.
flow.think: What else might be all around us, but too small or too clear to see?
flow.context: This is the last step of the sugar activity. You taste the water to check whether the sugar is still there.

activities.title: Cloudy Ice, Clear Ice

materials.item: two small steel bowls or ice trays
tap water
water that a grown-up has boiled and let cool
a freezer
a clean cloth and a rolling pin for crushing ice

activities.safety: Only a grown-up boils the water. Wrap ice in a cloth before crushing it, so no sharp bits fly.

schedule.what: Fill one bowl with tap water and one with boiled, cooled water. Freeze them overnight.
Compare the two ices. Look for bubbles. Crush some ice and see it turn white.

activities.record: Draw both pieces of ice. Mark where the cloudy parts are. Draw the crushed ice too.
activities.context: In this 2-day activity you freeze two bowls of water and see why ice is sometimes clear and sometimes cloudy. Then you crush ice and watch it turn white.

setup.art: Two steel bowls of water side by side, labelled TAP and BOILED, going into a freezer.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one bowl with tap water and one with boiled, cooled water. Freeze overnight.

setup.art: Two blocks of ice on a plate, one with a cloudy white middle full of tiny bubbles, one clearer.
setup.caption: 2. Next day, compare the two blocks of ice.

setup.art: Ice wrapped in a cloth being tapped with a rolling pin, and a heap of white crushed ice beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Crush some ice in a cloth. See it turn white.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils some water and lets it cool completely. 2. Fill one bowl with tap water and label it TAP. 3. Fill the other with the cooled boiled water and label it BOILED. 4. Put both in the freezer.
flow.say: Boiling pushes out some of the air hidden in water. Will that change the ice?
flow.kid: Fill one bowl with tap water. A grown-up gives you boiled, cooled water for the other. Freeze both.
flow.wait: Leave them in the freezer overnight
flow.context: This is the first step of the ice activity. You freeze two kinds of water to compare the ice.

flow.do: 1. Take out both ices and put them on a plate. 2. Hold each up to a window. 3. Look for tiny bubbles and cloudy parts.
flow.say: Look through each ice. Where is it clear? Where is it cloudy? What makes the cloudy parts?
flow.kid: Hold each ice up to the window. Where is it clear? Where is it cloudy? Look for bubbles.
flow.parent: The cloudy part is usually in the middle. Water freezes from the outside in, and pushes air into the middle, where it gets trapped as tiny bubbles. Boiled water often makes clearer ice, but it may still be cloudy in the middle. Either result is honest.

check.q: Why is the middle of the ice cloudy?
options: Tiny air bubbles scatter the light
check.why: Each tiny bubble has an edge where light bounces. Many bubbles make the ice cloudy, just like many sugar grains make sugar white. Picking 'dirty' is a natural guess, but melt the ice and the water is clean.

flow.context: This step of the ice activity compares the two ices and looks for the cloudy parts.

flow.do: 1. Wrap a piece of the clearest ice in a cloth. 2. Tap it with a rolling pin until it is crushed. 3. Open the cloth and look.
flow.say: That ice was nearly clear. Now look at it crushed. What colour is it?
flow.kid: Wrap ice in a cloth. Tap it to crush it. Open it. What colour is it now?
flow.think: Snow is made of clear ice. So why is snow white?
flow.context: This is the last step of the ice activity. You crush clear ice and see it turn white.

activities.title: Day Curtain, Night Curtain

materials.item: a window with a thin curtain, or a thin cotton saree hung over a window or a doorway
a room lamp or torch
a thick bedsheet or quilt

activities.safety: A grown-up goes outside with the child. Stay near the house, and only look into your own home.

schedule.what: In the daytime, look at the window from inside and from outside.
At night, with a lamp on inside, look again from outside. Then try a thick quilt.

activities.record: Draw the window four times: day from inside, day from outside, night from outside, and night with the quilt.
activities.context: In this 2-day activity you test a thin curtain by day and by night. You find out that it hides whoever is on the dim side, and shows whoever is on the bright side.

setup.art: A child inside a room behind a thin curtain in daytime, looking out at a bright street.
setup.caption: 1. In the day, sit behind a thin curtain and look out.

setup.art: A grown-up and child outside in daylight looking up at the same window, which shows only bright white cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Then go outside and look in. What can you see?

setup.art: The same window at night from outside, glowing, with a dark shape of a person moving behind the curtain.
setup.caption: 3. At night, with the lamp on inside, look in again.

flow.do: 1. In the daytime, your child sits inside behind a thin curtain. 2. They look out and say what they can see.
flow.say: What can you see outside through the curtain? Do you think anyone outside can see you?
flow.kid: Sit behind the thin curtain. What can you see outside? Can people see you?
flow.context: This is the first step of the day and night curtain activity. You look out through a thin curtain in the daytime.

flow.do: 1. One person stays inside behind the curtain and waves. 2. The other goes outside and looks at the window. 3. Swap.
flow.say: Can you see me waving? What does the curtain look like from out here?
flow.kid: Go outside with a grown-up. Look at the window. Can you see the person waving?
flow.parent: In the day, the person inside is usually hidden. The curtain looks bright from outside, because daylight bounces off it. If you live high up and cannot look in from outside, hang the saree in a doorway between two rooms. Light one room brightly and keep the other dim.
flow.context: This step of the curtain activity checks from outside, in the daytime, whether you can see in.

flow.do: 1. At night, switch on a lamp inside the room. 2. One person moves about behind the curtain. 3. The other goes outside and looks.
flow.say: It's the same curtain. Can you see in now? What changed?
flow.kid: Now it is night. The lamp is on inside. Look from outside. Can you see in?

check.q: At night, with the lamp on inside, people outside can see in. Why?
options: The curtain gets thinner at night
Now the room is the bright side
Curtains only work in the day
check.why: A thin curtain lets a little light through both ways. Whoever is on the bright side shows up to whoever is on the dark side. At night the room is the bright side. Picking 'thinner' usually means thinking the material changed. It is the light that changed.

flow.context: This step of the curtain activity looks at the window from outside at night, with a lamp on inside.

flow.do: 1. Hang a thick quilt or bedsheet over the window. 2. Look from outside again.
flow.say: Now with the thick quilt. Can you see anything?
flow.kid: Hang a thick quilt over the window. Look again. What can you see?
flow.think: Why do many homes have two curtains, one thin and one thick?
flow.context: This is the last step of the curtain activity. You add a thick, opaque quilt and look again.

activities.title: Act It Out: The Light Party

materials.item: an open space, like a room with the furniture pushed back
three paper signs: GLASS, BUTTER PAPER and STEEL PLATE

activities.safety: Walk, don't run, so nobody bumps heads.

schedule.what: Act out light going through glass, being scattered by butter paper, and being stopped by a steel plate.

activities.record: Draw yourself as light, going into each material.
activities.context: In this drama activity, one person acts as light and the others act as the atoms or threads of a material. You act out what happens in transparent, translucent and opaque materials.

setup.art: Children standing still with arms folded, as glass atoms, while another child walks straight past them.
setup.caption: 1. GLASS: the atoms keep their arms folded. They cannot catch the light, so it walks straight through.

setup.art: Children as paper threads gently turning a walking child this way and that, so they come out facing a new way.
setup.caption: 2. BUTTER PAPER: each thread turns the light a new way.

setup.art: Children with arms held out catching a 'light' child, who either turns back or sits down.
setup.caption: 3. STEEL PLATE: the atoms catch the light. It is sent back, or it sits down as warmth.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the GLASS sign. 2. Three people stand still, a step apart, with arms folded. 3. The 'light' walks straight past them from one side of the room to the other.
flow.say: This is glass. Its atoms cannot catch the light we see, so they keep their arms folded. The light walks straight through. Where does it come out?
flow.kid: You are light. Walk straight through the glass atoms. Don't turn. Where do you come out?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Light Party drama. You act out light going straight through glass.
flow.parent: The gaps are only so the light can walk. Real glass has no holes. Its atoms simply cannot absorb the light we see.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the BUTTER PAPER sign. 2. The atoms stand in a messy cluster. 3. When the 'light' reaches an atom, the atom gently turns it to face a new way. 4. The light keeps walking.
flow.say: This is butter paper. Every thread turns the light a new way. Did the light still get through? Did it come out where it was aiming?
flow.kid: Now the threads turn you gently, this way and that. Keep walking. Where do you come out?

check.q: In the butter paper game, the light got through but came out in a random place. What does that show?
options: Translucent things let light through but scatter it
check.why: The light got through, so it was not stopped. But it came out facing a new way, so the picture would be lost. That is translucent. Picking 'stop all light' mixes translucent up with opaque.

flow.context: This step of the Light Party drama acts out light being turned about inside butter paper.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the STEEL PLATE sign. 2. The atoms stand close together with arms held out. 3. When the light walks up, the atoms catch it. 4. The light either turns back, to show it is sent back, or sits down, to show it is absorbed.
flow.say: This is a steel plate. Its loose electrons catch the light. Most of it is sent back. A little is absorbed and warms the plate. None gets through.
flow.kid: Now the atoms catch you. You can't get through. Turn back, or sit down as warmth.
flow.think: If you were light, which material would you like to visit?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Light Party drama. You act out light being stopped by a steel plate.

projects.title: The Three-Light Lantern

materials.item: a sheet of thick card or a cereal box
butter paper or tracing paper
a piece of clear plastic from a used food box
glue, tape and child-safe scissors
a battery LED tealight, or a small torch lying on its side inside the box, pointing at the window you are testing

projects.safety: Use only a battery LED light inside the lantern, never a real flame or diya, because paper burns. A grown-up helps with cutting the windows.

schedule.what: Cut a box shape from card with four windows. Cover one window with clear plastic and two with butter paper. Cover the last one with card that has small holes in it, like a jaali.
Let the glue dry. Put the LED light inside in a dark room. Compare the light from each side on the wall.

projects.record: Draw what each side of the lantern shows on the wall. Label it transparent, translucent or opaque with holes.
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a lantern, like a Diwali kandil, with a different material on each side. Then you light it with an LED and see how each material changes the light on the wall.

setup.art: A flat cut-out card shape for a box with four square windows, on a table with scissors and glue.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a box shape from card, with a window in each side.

setup.art: The box being folded, one window covered with clear plastic, two with butter paper, one with a card jaali pattern of small holes.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the windows: clear plastic, butter paper, and a card jaali.

setup.art: The finished lantern glowing in a dark room: a sharp bright patch, a soft glow and a pattern of spots on the walls.
setup.caption: 3. Light it in the dark. Look at each wall.

flow.do: 1. Draw four 10 cm squares in a row on the card. 2. Add one more 10 cm square below the second square, for the bottom. 3. Cut out the shape. 4. A grown-up cuts a 6 cm window in each of the four side squares.
flow.say: This will fold into a box. Each side will get a different material, so we can compare them.
flow.kid: Draw the box shape. A grown-up helps cut the windows. Each side gets a different window.
flow.context: This is the first step of the lantern project. You cut out a box with a window on each side.

flow.do: 1. Glue clear plastic over window 1. 2. Glue butter paper over windows 2 and 3. 3. For window 4, glue on card with a pattern of small holes, like a jaali. 4. Fold and tape the box, leaving the top open.
flow.say: One clear window, two cloudy windows, and one blocked window with holes. Which will light the wall most? Which will make the softest light?
flow.kid: Glue clear plastic on one window. Butter paper on two. Card with holes on the last. Fold it into a box.
flow.context: This step of the lantern project covers each window with a different material.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Switch on the LED tealight and put it inside. 3. Put the lantern 30 cm from a wall. 4. Turn it so each side faces the wall in turn.
flow.say: Look at the wall. What does the clear side make? The butter paper side? The jaali side?
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Put the light inside. Turn each side to the wall. What do you see?

check.q: Which side made a soft, even glow with no sharp edges?
check.why: Butter paper scatters light in every direction, so the glow is soft and spread out. That is why lampshades and kandils are often made of translucent paper. The clear side makes a sharp, bright patch. The jaali makes a pattern of spots, because the card blocks light and the holes let it through.

flow.context: This step of the lantern project compares the light from each side in a dark room.

flow.do: Talk about where each kind of light is useful at home.
flow.say: Which side would you want for reading? For a baby's night light? For a party?
flow.kid: Which side is best for reading? For a sleepy baby? For a party?
flow.parent: Good answers: clear for bright reading light, butter paper for a soft night light, the jaali for a pretty pattern. Some children want to make the lantern with all translucent sides next.
flow.context: This is the last step of the lantern project. You decide which kind of light suits which job.

challenges.title: Keep the Light Out, Let Me See In
challenges.problem: Some medicines and milk spoil in light. Design a container that keeps light out, but still lets you check how much is left inside, without opening it.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
Test it in a dark room. Shine a torch on the covered side and look in through the open mouth. You should see no light inside.
You must be able to tell how full it is, without opening the lid.
materials: black paper, foil, card, cloth and tape
a torch, or a phone torch
general: Cover the whole bottle in black paper or foil, so it is opaque.
Leave a narrow strip from top to bottom, and cover it with a black paper flap. Lift the flap to see the water level, then close it.
Mark lines on the cover, and pour in water a cup at a time to learn which line each cup reaches.
creative: Brown and dark-green glass bottles let in less of the light that spoils things. That is why some medicine bottles are brown.
Shake it and listen. Does a full bottle sound different from a half-full one?
If you have a kitchen scale, weigh the bottle. A fuller bottle is heavier.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own container. Draw it, build it, and do the torch test in the dark. Can a friend tell how full it is without opening it?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You must make a container that is opaque to keep light out, but still lets you check what is inside.

setup.art: A clear plastic bottle half full of water on a table, beside black paper, foil and tape.
setup.caption: 1. Start with a clear bottle, half full of water.

setup.art: The bottle wrapped in black paper with a small flap cut in the side, lifted to show the water level.
setup.caption: 2. Make it opaque. Find a way to check the level.

setup.art: In a dark room, a grown-up shining a torch on the wrapped bottle while a child looks in through its open mouth.
setup.caption: 3. In the dark, shine a torch on the cover. Look inside. Any light getting in?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at a medicine bottle or milk packet at home.
flow.say: Why do you think this medicine bottle is brown, and this milk packet is not see-through?
flow.kid: Look at a medicine bottle or a milk packet. Is it see-through? Why not?
flow.context: This is the first step of the light-proof container challenge. You find out why some containers are not see-through.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a design. 2. They build it from the materials. 3. Fill the bottle halfway with water.
flow.say: Draw your idea first. How will you keep the light out? How will you check how full it is?
flow.kid: Draw your idea. Build it. Keep light out. Find a way to check how full it is.
flow.context: This step of the container challenge is for designing and building.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Take the lid off. 3. Shine the torch on the covered side, all the way round. 4. Your child looks in through the mouth for any light getting in.
flow.say: Is any light getting in? Where? How could you fix it?
flow.kid: In the dark, a grown-up shines a torch on the bottle. Look inside. Any light?

check.q: Light gets in where two pieces of black paper meet. What is the best fix?
options: Use a clear tape over the gap
Overlap the paper and cover the join with black tape
Leave a small gap so air can get in
check.why: Overlapping the paper and covering the join with black tape makes the whole cover opaque. Clear tape is transparent, so light would pass straight through it. Picking clear tape usually means thinking tape always seals light, but only opaque tape does.

flow.context: This step of the container challenge tests the container in the dark with a torch.

flow.do: Ask a friend or family member to say how full it is without opening the lid.
flow.say: Can they tell how full it is, without opening the lid? Did your design work?
flow.kid: Ask someone to guess how full it is. No opening the lid! Did it work?
flow.think: Can something be both opaque and easy to check? What did you trade?
flow.context: This is the last step of the container challenge. Someone checks whether your design lets them tell how full it is.

challenges.title: The Soft Night-Light
challenges.problem: A little cousin is scared of the dark, but a bare torch is too bright and hurts their eyes. Make a shade for an LED light that lights the whole room softly, with no bright spot you can see.
constraints: Use only an LED tealight or a torch, never a flame.
From across the room, nobody should see the bright point of the light.
The light should still be bright enough to see the door.
materials: an LED tealight, or a small torch
butter paper, tissue, a white plastic carry bag, a steel tumbler, an old white T-shirt, a clear plastic cup
general: Wrap a white plastic carry bag round the light, or stand a butter-paper tube over it. It scatters the light, so the bright point disappears.
Use more than one layer if the bright point still shows.
Point the light at a white wall and let the wall glow.
creative: Put the light inside a steel tumbler pointing up, with butter paper over the top. The tumbler sends light up and the paper spreads it.
Cut star holes in dark card wrapped around a butter-paper tube, for a night sky on the ceiling.
Stand the light behind a water-filled clear bottle with a little milk stirred in. The milk drops scatter the light into a soft glow.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own shade. Test it from across the room in the dark. Can you see the bright point? Can you see the door?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must use translucent materials to make a soft night-light, with no bright point that hurts the eyes.

setup.art: An LED tealight glowing alone on a shelf in a dark room, with a harsh bright point.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the bare LED from across a dark room.

setup.art: The same LED covered with a tube of butter paper, now glowing softly all over.
setup.caption: 2. Try covers of different translucent materials.

setup.art: A child in bed across the room, seeing a soft glow and the outline of the door.
setup.caption: 3. Test from across the room: no bright point, but you can see the door.

flow.do: In a dark room, put the bare LED on a shelf. Stand across the room and look.
flow.say: Can you see the bright point of the light? Does it hurt to look at?
flow.kid: Look at the bare light from across the dark room. Is it too bright?
flow.context: This is the first step of the night-light challenge. You see why a bare light can be too harsh.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries covering the LED with each material. 2. For each one, they check from across the room. 3. They pick the best and improve it.
flow.say: Try each material over the light. Which hides the bright point but still lights the room?
flow.kid: Try each cover. Check from across the room. Which hides the bright point?

check.q: Which cover will best hide the bright point but still let light out?
options: A steel tumbler over the light
check.why: Butter paper is translucent. It lets light through but scatters it, so the bright point vanishes into a soft glow. A clear cup is transparent, so you still see the point. A steel tumbler over the light is opaque, so almost no light gets out.

flow.context: This step of the night-light challenge tests different covers for the light.

flow.do: Build the final shade and test it in the dark.
flow.say: Can you see the door? Can you see the bright point?
flow.kid: Build your best shade. Test it in the dark. Can you see the door?
flow.context: This step of the night-light challenge builds and tests the final shade.

flow.do: Give the night-light to someone who might like it.
flow.say: Who would like this night-light? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: Who could use your night-light? What would you change next time?
flow.think: Why are so many lampshades made of translucent materials?
flow.context: This is the last step of the night-light challenge. You share your night-light and think about what to improve.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, holds three things up to the window: cling film, butter paper and a steel plate. Through which one will she see the neem tree outside clearly?
items.why: Cling film is transparent: light goes straight through, so the picture of the tree comes through too. Butter paper is translucent: light comes through, but it is scattered, so she sees only a glow. The steel plate is opaque: no light gets through at all.

items.p: A frosted bathroom window lets daylight in, but you cannot see the street through it. Which word describes frosted glass?
items.why: Light gets through, so it is not opaque. But the light is scattered, so no clear picture gets through, and it is not transparent. Translucent means light through, picture lost.

items.p: Sort these things into transparent, translucent and opaque.
items.a: see items
items.why: Ask two questions. Does light get through? Does a clear picture get through? Both yes: transparent. Light yes, picture no: translucent. No light: opaque.

items.p: Many people think that if light gets through something, you must be able to see through it. True or false?
items.why: False. Butter paper, frosted glass and a thin cotton cloth all let light through, but you cannot see a clear picture through them. They are translucent. Light can get through even when the picture cannot.

items.p: Revathi shines a torch at a wall, first through a sheet of butter paper, then through a steel plate. Predict what she will see on the wall each time. Explain why.
items.a: Through the butter paper, a soft, pale, blurry patch of light, because the paper lets light through but scatters it. Through the steel plate, a dark shadow, because steel is opaque and blocks all the light.
items.why: A strong answer predicts both results and gives the reason for each: scattered light for the translucent paper, blocked light for the opaque plate.

items.p: An opaque thing blocks light and leaves a dark patch behind it. This dark patch is called a ____.
items.why: A shadow is the place light cannot reach because something opaque is in the way. A translucent thing makes only a pale shadow.

items.p: In the gap test, Lakshmi could lift cling film 30 centimetres off the card before the word blurred. She could lift tissue only 1 centimetre. Which material scatters light more?
items.why: The more a material scatters light, the sooner the word blurs as you lift it. The tissue blurred the word after only 1 centimetre, so it scatters light much more. A strong answer reads the number as 'how far you could still read', not 'how much blur'.

items.p: In the gap test, Divya rests her chin on the same stack of books every time. Why does this make the test fair?
opts: Her eyes stay at the same height, so only the material changes
It helps her see in the dark
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If her eyes moved up or down between tries, the results could change for a reason that has nothing to do with the material.

items.p: Match each job to the kind of material it needs.
pairs: a box where shoppers can see the sweets inside
a paper lantern that spreads soft light
a curtain for a dark afternoon nap
a packet that keeps light away from milk
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Choose by what the job needs: a clear view (transparent), light without a picture (translucent), or no light at all (opaque).

items.p: In the Glowing Hands activity, you pressed a torch under your fingers in a dark room. What did you see? What does it tell you about your hand?
items.a: My fingers glowed red at the edges. So some light, mostly red light, can pass through my hand. No picture comes through, so my hand is a little translucent, not completely opaque.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child really saw, and uses it to say which group the hand belongs in.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out: a glass of clean water, a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a brick?
items.why: Clean water is transparent. The steel spoon, the wooden spoon and the brick are all opaque. A strong answer gives the reason, not just the pick.

items.p: Clear glass is completely invisible, because light goes straight through it.
items.why: False. You can still see a glass of water. A little light bounces off its surfaces, so you see shine, and its curved edges bend some light. That is how you can tell the glass is there.

items.p: Draw a torch shining at clear glass, butter paper and a wooden board, one at a time. Draw what you would see on the wall behind each one.
items.a: Behind the glass, a bright, sharp patch of light. Behind the butter paper, a soft, pale glow. Behind the wood, a dark shadow.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three different results: light straight through, light scattered, light blocked.
items.art: A torch on the left, three empty boxes for materials, and a blank wall on the right.

items.p: A family is choosing a new window for their bathroom. Three people want different things.

views.says: Clear glass. It lets in the most light, and I can see the sky.
Frosted glass. It lets in light, and nobody outside can see in.
A wooden shutter with a carved jaali. Air comes in, the holes make patterns of light, and the wood keeps us private.

items.ask: Which window would you choose for a bathroom? Give a reason using the words transparent, translucent or opaque. Then say one thing another person's window does better.
items.a: A strong answer picks one window and explains it with how the material treats light. For example, frosted glass is translucent, so light comes in but the picture is lost. It then gives a fair point for another choice: clear glass lets in more light, and a jaali lets in air. The best answers notice that a bathroom needs privacy first, but that each choice gives something up.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each material is a trade-off between light, view, privacy and air.

items.p: Asha says, 'With dark sunglasses on, I can look straight at the Sun safely.' Is she right?
opts: Yes, dark lenses block enough light
No. Sunglasses only cut part of the light. Never look straight at the Sun, with or without them.
Yes, but only in the morning
items.why: Sunglasses are tinted: they let part of the light through. The Sun is so bright that even that part can harm the eyes. Never look straight at the Sun.

items.p: Thenmozhi puts a drop of coconut oil on a piece of white paper. The spot becomes see-through. What did the oil do?
opts: It turned the paper into glass
It filled the air gaps between the paper's threads, so light bounced less
items.why: Paper is a tangle of threads with air between them. Light bounces at every edge between thread and air, which scatters it. Oil fills the gaps, so there are far fewer edges. The paper is just as thick as before.

items.p: Predict: if you dip a white cotton handkerchief in water, will it become more see-through or less? Explain using what you found in the Oil Spot Window.
items.a: More see-through. Cotton is threads with air between them, like paper. Water fills the air gaps, so light bounces at fewer edges and more light comes straight through. When the cloth dries, it will go back to how it was.
items.why: A strong answer uses the air-gap idea from the oil-spot test to predict a new material.

items.p: Lakshmi stirs a spoon of white sugar into a glass of water. The water stays clear. Has the sugar gone?
opts: No. It has split into pieces too tiny to scatter light. The water tastes sweet.
items.why: A heap of sugar looks white because light bounces off the edges of every grain. Stirred in, the sugar splits into molecules far too small to scatter light, so the water looks clear. Tasting shows the sugar is still there.

items.p: Farida crushes a clear ice cube into many tiny bits. Predict the colour of the heap.
items.why: Each bit of ice has edges where light bounces. So many edges scatter light in every direction, and the heap looks white. Snow is white for the same reason.

items.p: Thick glass, like the heavy bottom of a glass tumbler, often looks greenish and less clear than a thin windowpane.
items.why: True. Glass soaks up a tiny bit of light, a little more of some colours. In thin glass you hardly notice. Through thick glass, it adds up. How see-through a thing is depends on how thick it is.

items.p: In the Sunglasses Lab, Priya could read row 5 of the chart outdoors with sunglasses on. Indoors with them on, she could read only row 2. What explains this?
opts: Sunglasses let only part of the light through, and indoors there is little light to start with
items.why: Sunglasses cut the light. In bright sun that helps. Indoors there is not much light, so cutting it makes reading harder. The chart stayed the same, so the letters did not change.

items.p: Why are some medicine bottles brown or white and opaque, and not clear?
items.a: Light can spoil some medicines. A brown or opaque bottle keeps most of the light out, so the medicine stays good for longer.
items.why: A strong answer links the material's choice to its job: stopping light reaching what is inside.

items.p: Put these in order, from most see-through to least: one sheet of butter paper, two sheets on top of each other, four sheets, eight sheets.
items.why: Every extra sheet adds more edges that scatter light and more paper that soaks some up. So the more sheets, the less light gets through. A thick enough pile would be nearly opaque. Being see-through depends on thickness.

items.p: Each of these is made of something clear, yet looks white. Match each one to why.
pairs: the cloudy middle of an ice cube
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In every case, light bounces off many tiny edges between the clear material and air, so it scatters in all directions and looks white.

items.p: Three people argue about whether your hand is opaque.

views.says: My hand is opaque. I cannot see anything through it, and it makes a dark shadow.
My hand is translucent. In the dark, my fingers glowed red over the torch.

views.who: A doctor who looks at X-ray photos
views.says: For X-rays, the soft parts of a hand are nearly transparent, and only the bones block them.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give evidence from the Glowing Hands activity. Then say why one of the others also has a point.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with evidence, for example the red glow at the edges of the fingers. It then gives the other side fairly: for ordinary daylight, a hand does block almost everything and makes a dark shadow. The best answers say that the answer depends on the kind of light and how thick the part of the hand is.
items.why: All three are partly right. Whether something is opaque depends on the kind of light and the thickness, not only on the material.

items.p: In the Three-Light Lantern, which side made a pattern of bright spots on the wall?
opts: The card jaali side with holes
items.why: The card is opaque, so it blocks light everywhere except at the holes. Light goes through the holes in straight lines and makes spots in the same pattern. A stone jaali makes patterns of light on a floor the same way.

items.p: Butter paper sends the light that passes through it bouncing off in many different ____. This is called scattering.
items.why: When light is scattered, the light from each point of a picture gets mixed up with the light from other points, so the picture is lost.

items.p: Draw a window with a thin curtain twice: once in the day, and once at night with a lamp on inside. Show who can see whom.
items.a: Day: the person inside can see the street, but the street sees only a bright curtain. Night: the street can see the person's shape, but the person sees only the curtain.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the rule: whoever is on the bright side is seen by whoever is on the dim side.
items.art: Two blank window frames side by side, labelled DAY and NIGHT.

items.p: Which pair of sunglasses protects your eyes better on a sunny beach in Chennai?
opts: Very dark ones with no label
Both the same, because darker is always safer
items.why: Ultraviolet light from the Sun can harm the eyes, and we cannot see it. A UV400 label means the lenses block it. Very dark lenses without it can be worse, because the pupils open wide in the dark and let more ultraviolet light in. Darker is not always safer.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 4, says, 'Snow is white because it is made of a white kind of ice.' What is wrong with his idea? How could you show it at home?
items.a: Snow is made of ordinary clear ice. It looks white because millions of tiny crystals scatter the light. I could show it by crushing a clear ice cube: the bits look white, though they are the same ice.
items.why: A strong answer finds the mistake (the ice is not white), gives the real reason (many tiny edges) and names a test.

items.p: Will a few drops of water make each of these clearer to see through, or make no difference?
items: the rough side of a frosted glass window
items.a: see items
items.why: Water helps only when the material scatters light at tiny air gaps or a rough surface: it fills them. Steel and wood soak up or bounce back the light, so filling gaps cannot help.

items.p: Why is glass see-through, but a steel plate is not?
opts: Glass has tiny holes in it
The electrons in glass cannot soak up the light we see, but metal has loose electrons that catch it
items.why: In glass, the light we see does not have the right energy for the electrons to soak it up, so it passes by. Metals have loose electrons that catch light and send it back. A common guess is holes, but glass has no holes you could see through.

items.p: Meera sits by a closed glass window in the sun all afternoon. Why is she unlikely to get sunburnt?
opts: Window glass blocks much of the Sun's ultraviolet light
items.why: Sunburn is caused mainly by ultraviolet light, which we cannot see. Window glass lets the light we see through, but stops much of the ultraviolet. So glass is transparent to one kind of light and nearly opaque to another.

items.p: A brick wall is opaque, so no kind of light can pass through it.
items.why: False. Brick blocks the light we see, but radio waves and Wi-Fi signals, which are kinds of light we cannot see, pass through it. That is why a phone works indoors. Opaque always means opaque to a certain kind of light.

items.p: Glass frogs live in rainforests in Central and South America. When a glass frog sleeps, the frog becomes more see-through. How?
opts: They pack most of their red blood cells into their liver
They drink a lot of water
items.why: Scientists found this in 2022. Red blood is easy to spot, so while they sleep the frog hides most of their red blood cells in the liver. When they wake, the blood flows out again.

items.p: For about the first 380,000 years after the Big Bang, light could not travel far through the universe. What was the universe like?
items.why: The early universe was hot and full of loose particles that light kept bumping into, like light in fog. When it cooled and atoms formed, it became transparent. 'Dark and empty' is a natural guess, but it was glowing hot.

items.p: Many people say old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downwards over hundreds of years. Is this true?
items.why: False. Old glass was made unevenly, and builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Some old panes have the thick edge at the top. Scientists worked out that glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag enough to see.

items.p: Light made deep in the centre of the Sun reaches the Sun's surface within a few seconds.
items.why: False. The inside of the Sun is so crowded that light keeps bumping into particles and changing direction, like a person trying to cross a packed crowd. Estimates for how long it takes range from about 10,000 to 170,000 years.

items.p: A gold coin is opaque. Gold beaten into gold leaf, thinner than paper, lets a little greenish light through. What does this tell you about whether 'opaque' is fixed for a material?
items.a: It is not fixed. The same gold is opaque when it is thick and lets light through when it is very thin. So being opaque depends on thickness, not only on what a thing is made of.
items.why: A strong answer uses the gold example to make a general rule, and may add another example, like many sheets of butter paper.

items.p: Scientists have argued about what glass really is.

views.says: Glass is a solid. It is stiff, and windows keep their shape for hundreds of years.
Glass is more like a liquid that has got stuck. Its atoms are jumbled in no neat order, like the atoms of a liquid.
Glass is its own kind of material, in between, and how it becomes stiff as it cools is still being studied.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing? Give your reason. Then say what evidence the other side would point to.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and gives evidence, for example that window glass does not sag or flow, so it acts like a solid. It then states the other side fairly: inside, its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's, unlike the neat rows in salt or ice. The best answers say both facts are true, which is why the question is hard.
items.why: This is a real open question. Glass acts like a solid but is arranged like a liquid, so each side points to true evidence.

items.p: In the gap test, butter paper let you read the word when it touched the card, but not when you lifted it 2 centimetres. Explain why.
items.a: Butter paper scatters light only a little. When it touches the card, the light from each letter has no room to spread before it comes through. When it is lifted, the scattered light spreads out over a wider patch, and the letters blur into each other.
items.why: A strong answer says that the further scattered light travels, the more it spreads. That is why tracing paper works only when it lies flat on the picture.

items.p: In 1938, Katharine Burr Blodgett invented a very thin coating for glass. With it, glass bounced back almost no light. Why did this make the glass clearer?
opts: More light went through, instead of bouncing off
The coating made the glass thinner
The coating made its own light
items.why: Ordinary glass bounces back a little light at each surface, which makes a faint shine and reflections. Her coating stopped most of that bounce, so more light went through. Coatings like hers are used on camera lenses and spectacles today.

items.p: For each thing, do we want it transparent, translucent or opaque?
items: the front of a fish tank
a lampshade for a reading lamp
a cover for a bird cage at night
items.a: see items
items.why: We choose a material by what the job needs: a clear view, soft light without glare, or darkness. A strong sorter can say the job behind each choice.

items.p: Why do birds sometimes fly into a clean glass window?
opts: The glass is transparent, so the bird sees the trees through the glass and not the glass itself
Birds like the shine on glass
The glass is opaque to birds
items.why: Clean glass lets most light straight through, so the view behind the glass looks like open space. Sticking patterns or stickers on windows helps birds see that the glass is there.

items.p: Invent a new use for a material that lets one kind of light through but blocks another kind.
items.a: Any idea with a clear reason. For example: a window that lets in the light we see but blocks heat from the Sun, so rooms stay cool in summer.
items.why: Real engineers make glass like this. A strong answer names which kind of light passes, which is blocked, and why that helps.

items.p: At night, a thin curtain shows you to the street when your lamp is on. Without buying a thicker curtain, give two ways to keep your room private in the evening. Explain each one.
items.a: For example: switch off the lamp near the window and use a small lamp further inside, so the room is less bright than the street. Or hang a thick opaque cloth, like a razai, over the window at night. Or keep a light on outside the window so the outside is the bright side.
items.why: A strong answer uses the rule that the bright side is the one that shows, or uses an opaque material to block the light.

items.p: Match each material to what it mostly does to light.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Light that meets a material can pass straight through, be scattered, be absorbed or bounce back. Most materials do a mix. The biggest part decides how the material looks.
