quiz.p: Through which of these could you read a newspaper clearly?
quiz.why: The clear plastic cover is transparent, so the picture of the words comes through. Butter paper scatters the light, so the words blur. Cardboard blocks the light.

quiz.p: A paper lantern glows when the bulb inside is on, but you cannot see the shape of the bulb. The paper is…
quiz.why: Light comes through the paper, but scattered, so the picture of the bulb is lost. That is translucent.

quiz.p: Which of these makes the darkest shadow on the wall?
quiz.why: The steel tumbler is opaque and blocks all the light. Butter paper makes a pale shadow, and a glass tumbler hardly any.

quiz.p: In the gap test, why do we try each material three times?
opts: Because one try can be a fluke
Because three is a lucky number
quiz.why: A hand can wobble, or someone can say 'stop' too late. Three tries, and taking the middle result, give a fairer answer.

quiz.p: In the gap test, the plastic bag could be lifted 6 cm before the word blurred, and the butter paper only 2 cm. How many times higher was the plastic bag?
quiz.why: 6 divided by 2 is 3. So the plastic bag could be lifted 3 times as high. Picking 4 usually means subtracting, 6 take away 2, instead of dividing.

quiz.p: Why does wet paper let more light through than dry paper?
opts: Water fills the air gaps between the threads, so light bounces less
quiz.why: Light scatters at every edge between paper and air. Water fills those gaps, so more light goes straight through.

quiz.p: A heap of salt looks white, but one big salt crystal is see-through. Why?
opts: The heap has many tiny edges that scatter light
The heap is made of a different salt
quiz.why: Each grain has edges where light bounces. Many grains scatter light in all directions, so the heap looks white. One big crystal has few edges.

quiz.p: Kavya is packing Pongal sweets in boxes. She wants shoppers to see the sweets without opening the box. Which lid should she use?
quiz.why: To see the sweets, the lid must let a clear picture through, so it must be transparent.

quiz.p: Why do sunglasses help on a bright, sunny day?
opts: They let only part of the light through, so there is less glare
They make the Sun safe to look at
quiz.why: Sunglasses are tinted. They cut the bright light so your eyes are comfortable, and good ones also block ultraviolet light. They never make it safe to look at the Sun.

quiz.p: In the daytime, Meenu sits in her dim room behind a thin curtain. The lane outside is bright. Who can see whom?
opts: Meenu can see the lane, but the lane cannot see her
The lane can see Meenu, but she cannot see out
quiz.why: Through a thin curtain, you can see from the dim side into the bright side. By day the lane is the bright side, so Meenu sees out and stays hidden.

quiz.p: One sheet of tissue paper is translucent. What happens if you stack twenty sheets?
quiz.why: Each sheet scatters and soaks up some light. With twenty sheets, almost no light gets through. Being see-through depends on thickness.

quiz.p: Which question about glass do scientists still argue about?
opts: What kind of material glass really is, deep down
quiz.why: Everyone agrees glass is transparent and can break. But glass is stiff like a solid while its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's, and scientists still study what kind of material that makes it.

quiz.p: When you press a torch under your fingers in the dark, which colour of light gets through your hand the most?
quiz.why: Skin and blood soak up most colours, but red light gets through best. That is why your fingers glow red.

applications: Windows of glass let in light and a view, while keeping out wind, rain and dust.
Frosted and patterned glass in bathrooms and office doors lets light in but keeps privacy.
Thin curtains soften bright sun. Thick blackout curtains make rooms dark for sleep.
Sunglasses cut glare and block ultraviolet light. Welders wear very dark glass to protect their eyes from the blinding welding arc.
Opaque and brown bottles protect medicines, milk and cooking oil from light that spoils them.
Lampshades, kandils and paper lanterns use translucent materials to spread light softly.
Greenhouses use transparent or translucent covers so plants get light and stay warm.
Spectacles, camera lenses and phone screens need very transparent glass or plastic.
Stone jaalis in Indian buildings let in light and air but keep rooms cool and private.
Shadow-puppet artists, such as tholu bommalata puppeteers in Andhra Pradesh, use translucent painted leather so the audience sees coloured shadows.
Tracing paper and butter paper let you copy a picture by laying the paper on top.
Optical fibres of very clear glass carry internet signals as light under the oceans.
Scientists slice rocks so thin that light passes through, to study what they are made of.
Food packets for chips and biscuits are opaque, often lined with metal foil, to keep light and air out.

open_questions.why_open: Its atoms are in no neat order, like a liquid's, but it is stiff like a solid. How a liquid becomes glass as it cools is still one of the big puzzles of physics.

open_questions.q: What is dark matter, the matter that light passes straight through?
open_questions.why_open: It pulls on stars and galaxies, so we know something is there. But big experiments have not yet caught a single particle of it.

open_questions.q: How does a glass frog keep their blood from clotting when they pack it into their liver?
open_questions.why_open: In people, packed blood would clot dangerously. The frog does this every night and wakes up fine. Scientists are still studying how.

open_questions.q: When a packet of light reaches a window, what decides whether it goes through or bounces back?
open_questions.why_open: Only the share can be predicted. Most physicists say each packet is pure chance. Some think hidden details might decide. Experiments have not settled what this chance really is.

open_questions.q: Exactly how long does light take to escape from the middle of the Sun?
open_questions.why_open: Estimates range from about 10,000 to 170,000 years, because it depends on details of the Sun's inside that we cannot measure directly.

open_questions.q: Could we make walls or cars that are see-through, but strong?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made see-through wood and see-through ceramics. Making them cheap and strong enough for everyday use is still being worked on.

Why does fog hide the trees?

What does 'I can see right through you' mean, when people say it?

maths.problem: In the gap test, the plastic bag could be lifted 6 cm before the word blurred. The butter paper could be lifted only 2 cm. How many times higher was the plastic bag?
maths.explain: The plastic bag could be lifted to 6 cm. The butter paper only to 2 cm. 6 divided by 2 is 3. So the plastic bag went 3 times as high. You can check: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
maths.context: This is about the gap test. You lay a material on a card of big letters and lift it slowly. You measure how high it goes before the word blurs. Higher means more see-through.
maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'the bag is more see-through'. They ask 'how much more?' Dividing tells us: this many times.

maths.problem: In the gap test, the handkerchief's three tries were 4 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order: 2, 3, 4. The middle one is 3. So the middle value is 3 cm.
maths.context: This is about the gap test, where you test each material 3 times and take the middle value. You lift each material off a card of letters and measure when the word blurs.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. Putting three tries in order and taking the middle one gives a fairer answer.

maths.problem: In the oil spot experiment, each spot gets a score from 0 to 3. The dry spot scored 1, the water spot scored 2, and the oil spot scored 3. After one hour, the water spot scored 1. By how much did the water spot's score drop?
maths.explain: The water spot first scored 2. After an hour it scored 1. 2 take away 1 is 1. So it dropped by 1, back to the same as the dry spot.
maths.context: This is about the oil spot experiment. You put drops of water and oil on paper, lay it on a newspaper, and score each spot from 0, where you see nothing of the print, to 3, where you can read the words.

chart.title: See-through score straight away and after one hour

maths.why_maths: Taking one score from another shows how much something changed. Here it shows the water drying away.

maths.problem: The Three-Light Lantern has 4 side windows. One is clear plastic, two are butter paper, and one is a card jaali. What fraction of the windows are butter paper?
maths.answer: Two quarters, which is the same as one half.
maths.explain: There are 4 windows. 2 of them are butter paper. So 2 out of 4 are butter paper. That is two quarters. Two quarters is the same as one half.
maths.context: This is about the lantern project, where you build a box lantern with a different material on each of its 4 sides and light it with an LED.
maths.why_maths: Fractions tell us what part of the whole is made of each material. That helps you plan how much of each to cut.

maths.problem: Dark sunglasses let through about 1 out of every 10 parts of the light that hits them. If 100 parts of light hit the lenses, about how many get through?
maths.explain: 1 out of every 10 parts gets through. 100 is 10 groups of 10. One from each group is 10. So about 10 parts of light get through, and about 90 are stopped.
maths.context: This is about the sunglasses lab, where you read a letter chart with and without sunglasses. Sunglasses are tinted, so they let only part of the light through.
maths.why_maths: Sharing into equal groups shows how much light the lenses really let through. That explains why the letters are hard to read in a dim room.

roots.context: We have been learning how light goes straight through some things, is scattered by others, and is stopped by the rest. Now we ask what this tells us about seeing, and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: Butter paper lying on a word lets you read it. Lift it 2 cm, and the paper still glows, but the word is gone. The paper scatters the light from each letter in every direction, mixing it with light from the others. So a frosted window lets in light but shows no view: it mixes up the light from everything outside.
deep_truth.habit: We think we can see through something whenever light gets through it. A frosted bathroom window is bright, yet it shows no view, so light alone is not enough.
deep_truth.evidence: In the gap test, butter paper lying on the card let you read the word. Lifted 2 cm, it still glowed with light, but the word was gone.

three.who_am_i: Your hand looks opaque, yet red light passes through your fingers. Even you are a little translucent.
three.what_is_life: Some animals hide by being almost transparent. A sleeping glass frog even packs most of their red blood cells into their liver while they sleep.
three.what_is_this_world: The whole universe was once like a thick fog. Then it cleared, and light could travel. We still see that first clear light today.

roots.thread: Everything comes from one source and is connected. In this unit, the same torch light met glass, butter paper and a steel plate. Glass let it pass, butter paper scattered it, and steel sent it back or absorbed it. The light did not change, and neither did the materials. Transparent, translucent and opaque name what happens when the two meet.

teachings.teaching: A father, Uddalaka, asks his son to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the son cannot see the salt. But every sip tastes salty. The father says: in the same way, what is finest is everywhere, unseen. 'You are that.'
teachings.link: Sugar stirred into water becomes clear and invisible, but it is still there in every sip. Not seeing something does not mean it is not there.

teachings.teaching: The face of truth is covered by a golden lid. The seeker asks for the lid to be taken away, so the truth can be seen.
teachings.link: A golden lid is opaque. Gold sends light back, so it hides what is under it, however beautiful it looks. The verse asks what might be covering what is true.

teachings.teaching: 'For now we see through a glass, darkly.' The Greek word Paul used means a mirror. Mirrors then were polished metal, and showed only a dim, blurry picture. Paul says what we know now is like that picture, and one day we may see clearly.
teachings.link: In this unit, a blurry picture came from light being scattered on its way. An old metal mirror blurred for a similar reason: its surface was never perfectly smooth. Paul uses that blur to say that what we know now is not yet the clear view.

science.text: Whether a material is see-through depends on its thickness, its tiny edges and the kind of light. Glass passes the light we see but stops much ultraviolet light. A brick wall stops the light we see but lets radio waves through.
For about 380,000 years, the young universe was opaque, like fog. Then it became transparent, and that first light still reaches us.

other_view.who: The Charvaka thinkers of ancient India, and many scientists today
other_view.view: Transparency is just atoms and light, and nothing more. There is no one source behind it. Light passes through glass because of electrons and energy, and that is the whole story. This is an honest view, and many careful people hold it.

practice.say: Let's stand at a window together. First, look at the glass. Can you find a speck of dust, or a smudge? Now let your eyes go through the glass, to the farthest thing you can see. Breathe slowly three times. Did you stop noticing the glass? It was there the whole time. Now hold your fingers together up to the bright sky, never towards the Sun. Can you see a thin red glow between them?

how_we_found_out.story: It seems obvious that white paper hides what is behind it because paper is a blocking material. Isaac Newton, an English scientist, looked more carefully. In his book Opticks, published in 1704, he described simple observations. Clear glass, ground into a powder, turns white, and you cannot see through it. Foam is made of clear water and clear air, yet it is white. Paper soaked in water or oil becomes much more see-through. Newton argued that the tiny parts of almost every material let some light through. A thing looks white or opaque because light bounces off the many edges between its tiny parts and the gaps around them. Fill the gaps with water or oil, and there are fewer edges to bounce from, so more light goes straight through. So the old idea was wrong. What hides the view is often the edges inside a thing, not what it is made of. You can check this yourself with one drop of oil on a sheet of paper.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: White paper and other opaque things block light because their material blocks light. Newton showed that powdered clear glass turns white, and oiled paper turns see-through, so the many inside edges do the blocking.
